t: #3490 Count Beautiful Numbers — Digit DP Tracking (sum, product)
o: A number is beautiful iff digit-product is divisible by digit-sum. The range goes up to 1e9, so we count f(x) = beautiful numbers in [1, x] with a digit DP and answer f(r) − f(l−1). The obstacle is the product, which seems unbounded — but with at most 9 digits the product is at most 9⁹ ≈ 3.9·10⁸, small enough to be a DP dimension directly. Leading zeros must not contribute (they'd zero the product spuriously), hence a "started" flag; once started, a zero digit makes the product 0, which is divisible by any positive sum — those branches are automatically handled since 0 % s == 0.
k: Digit DP over (position, sum, product, tight, started); product ≤ 9⁹ fits easily in 64 bits.
Leading zeros are skipped via the started flag so the product stays neutral (1) before the number begins.
Answer = f(r) − f(l−1), the standard inclusive-range trick.

a.n: Approach 1: Digit DP with Exact Product
a.i: Walk the digits of x; at each position try digits 0..hi (hi bounded by tightness). Unstarted zeros keep state (sum 0, product 1); started digits accumulate sum and multiply product. At the end accept iff started and product % sum == 0. Memoize on (i, sum, product, tight, started); the reachable (sum, product) pairs number only in the thousands, so the cache stays small.
s: Define dp(i, s, p, tight, started).
Accept at i == n iff started and p % s == 0.
a.t: O(digits · states) — states are (i ≤ 10) × (sum ≤ 81) × distinct products (few thousand) × 4 flags

w: The key realization is that 9 digits bound the product to ~4·10⁸, letting us carry it exactly instead of inventing clever modular tricks. Never let leading zeros enter the product — the started flag exists precisely for that. Edge cases: l = 1 (f(0) = 0) and single-digit numbers, all of which are beautiful. Follow-up: raise the bound to 10¹⁸ — then you must track the product modulo candidate sums or exploit that a zero digit trivializes everything.
